tasks.locator: Results › CSF Monoamine Metabolites › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 (p. 133)
tasks.extracted: Lumbar CSF 5-HIAA was 10.3 (SD 3.1) ng/ml in 30 people who had used MDMA at least 25 times vs 15.2 (7.9; range 4.8 to 37.3) in 28 controls; ANCOVA with age and height F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001; group x gender ANCOVA group F(1, 52) = 14.9, p < .001. Editors' calculation: about 32% lower; unadjusted difference 4.9 ng/ml (95% CI 1.7 to 8.1).

tasks.locator: Results › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 and its footnotes (p. 133)
tasks.extracted: The difference depended on sex (group x gender F(1, 52) = 5.1, p < .03): 46% lower in women (10.1 vs 18.7 ng/ml; 12 vs 11), marked significant, and 20% lower in men (10.8 vs 13.4; 18 vs 17), not marked significant in Table 4. Control women had higher 5-HIAA than control men.
CSF 5-HIAA was not significantly related to the number of MDMA exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33), duration or frequency of use, or time since last use (coefficients not given).

Lifetime use of other drug classes, MDMA group (30) vs controls (28): cocaine 24 (80%) vs 8 (29%); LSD and other hallucinogens 26 (87%) vs 9 (32%); benzodiazepines 18 (60%) vs 6 (21%); sedative-hypnotics 10 (33%) vs 1 (4%); non-MDMA amphetamines 13 (43%) vs 4 (14%); opiates 16 (53%) vs 9 (32%); cannabis 28 (93%) vs 22 (printed 73%).

The authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone and base the neurotoxicity reading on similar CSF 5-HIAA decrements in MDMA-treated monkeys with known serotonin deficits; they describe the controls as matched for age, height, weight, gender, education and other drug use.
Prolactin responses before and after intravenous L-tryptophan showed gender effects but no significant drug effects on peak change or area under the curve.

tasks.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 279); Table 3 (p. 280)
tasks.extracted: Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall learning and memory g -1.37 (95% CI -2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; current vs MDMA-naive: g -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%.

Verbal memory subtests vs MDMA-naive groups: abstinent immediate -1.22 (-3.63 to 1.18) and delayed -1.30 (-4.15 to 1.54), 3 studies each, I2 94 to 96%; current immediate -0.41 (-0.88 to 0.06) and delayed -1.16 (-2.58 to 0.26). All four intervals include zero.

tasks.locator: Results › Patterns of MDMA use and other drug use, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276, continues p. 279)
tasks.extracted: Polysubstance use: in all studies both MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too; two used alcohol- and tobacco-using controls, and only one (Taurah et al., 2014) a completely drug-naive comparison group.

Quality: all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies rated poor, 5 fair; comparability of abstinent and control groups questioned in all studies and matching in all case-control studies; exposure assessed by self-report in 12 of 14.

Overall conclusion: deficits seem particularly evident in updating of verbal and visuospatial material and in visuospatial tasks with high executive demand; shifting appears relatively immune; evidence for inhibition and access to long-term memory is weak and ambiguous.

tasks.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Updating: 9 studies, all but one by some combination of the review's authors; 7 reported computation span deficits; of 5 reporting span scores, the largest difference was 2.48 span items (2.75 in people abstinent for at least 6 months vs 5.23 in polydrug controls). Samples overlap: 27 of 44 people in one study were also in another.

Only one included study was genuinely prospective (people tested before first ecstasy use); the others were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental, which makes it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences; the reviewers argue that prospective studies are slow and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical.

As summarized by the review: a meta-analysis of 26 studies with calculable effect sizes (Laws and Kokkalis, 2007) gave Cohen's d of -0.63 for short-term memory, -0.87 for long-term memory, -1.00 for verbal memory and -0.27 for visual memory; a review of over one hundred neurocognitive studies (Rogers et al., 2009) found differences against both people who do not use drugs and people who use other drugs, varying in strength by task; a third review (Nulsen et al., 2010) reported poorer performance in all memory domains.

tasks.locator: §3.5 Neurocognition: the contributory role of other psychoactive drugs, 3rd paragraph (proof lines 587-605)
tasks.extracted: As summarized: in the same review (Rogers et al., 2009), seven variables had enough studies for meta-analysis; on all six memory measures (RAVLT immediate and delayed word recall, Rivermead immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) the ecstasy group scored lower than both people who do not use drugs and people who use other drugs, while the seventh, IQ, did not differ from the polydrug comparison group; differences were generally largest against people who do not use drugs.

tasks.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
tasks.extracted: As summarized by the letter from the same meta-analysis: marked variation across studies; pooled digit span lower than in people who use other drugs (P=0.017); a pooled verbal immediate-recall composite lower over 27 published studies (P<0.001); 6 of the 7 meta-analysed variables lower, with NART IQ the exception.

As summarized: a review of 33 published studies of working memory (Murphy et al., 2009) found performance normal in most studies, executive-shifting and most inhibition tasks unaffected, and differences mainly on tasks requiring the updating of verbal information and on visuospatial tasks needing processing beyond storage and retrieval.

The review states that many simple cognitive skills are not affected and that even on tasks that often show differences these are not universally found: in the meta-analysis it cites, individual studies of digit span and of a verbal immediate-recall composite were a mixture of significant and non-significant results although the pooled estimates were significant; the author attributes the variation to lifetime dose, sample size, participant selection and control of error variance.

Of about 1500 people screened by telephone, about 250 qualified for baseline, 116 completed testing and 5 were excluded for drugs found in hair or urine, leaving 52 people who had used ecstasy and 59 who had not; criteria were relaxed for 6 people.

Memory measures did not differ after adjustment: CVLT trials 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, difference -0.5 (95% CI -4.2 to 3.2), p = 0.79; WMS-III logical memory immediate 0.7 (-3.6 to 5.0) and delayed 0.7 (-2.4 to 3.8); verbal paired associates delayed 0.1 (-0.7 to 0.8); Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall 0.8 (-1.8 to 3.4).

Significant (uncorrected) whole-group differences: vocabulary 4.7 (1.1 to 8.4), p = 0.01; digit symbol 7.1 (1.0 to 13.2), p = 0.02; spatial span forward 0.8 (0.0 to 1.6), p = 0.04; non-dominant-hand pegboard -5.0 s (-9.3 to -0.7), p = 0.02; borderline Raven's (p = 0.05) and digits backwards (p = 0.05); verbal IQ 6.0 (-0.2 to 12.2), p = 0.06.

tasks.locator: Table 3 (comparison vs heavier-use columns); Results, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Heavier use (more than 50 episodes, n = 22) vs no use: fewer brief items on the Revised Strategy Application Test, 79.5 vs 88.5%, difference 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = 0.003, virtually unchanged after further adjustment for verbal IQ and depression score; slower non-dominant-hand pegboard, -8.4 s (-13.9 to -2.8), p = 0.003; lower vocabulary 5.0 (0.2 to 9.8), p = 0.04; no other differences.

Within the ecstasy group, more lifetime episodes (log-transformed) went with fewer brief items: coefficient -1.4 (-2.3 to -0.4), p = 0.004, adjusted for age, gender and race/ethnicity; Pearson r = -0.37; not driven by outliers on inspection of the scatterplot.

For heavier use vs no use, the largest effect not excluded at the 0.05 level ranged from Cohen's d 0.37 (Wisconsin perseverations) to 0.76 (spatial span total) on 14 chosen measures; the authors say a large effect (d 0.8) could be excluded on all of them and a medium effect (d 0.5) on many.

The authors read the lower vocabulary as a premorbid difference, since vocabulary is generally preserved after neurological insults, and the differences seen only with lighter use, and the pegboard difference, as likely chance; strategic self-regulation is their only consistent finding, possibly reflecting reflection impulsivity, which they say may predate use.

The ecstasy group more often had parents with high-school education or less (father 53.9% vs 27.1%, p = 0.006; mother 61.5% vs 27.1%, p < 0.001), was less often white (76.9% vs 91.5%, p = 0.04), had attended more all-night parties (median 98 vs 45, p = 0.005) and reported more marijuana intoxications (median 10 vs 1, p < 0.001).

As listed by the letter from the study's Table 2: Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span forwards P<0.04, WAIS digit-symbol P<0.02, WAIS vocabulary P<0.01, WAIS digits backwards P<0.05 and grooved pegboard with the non-dominant hand P<0.02. The letter rejects the study authors' reading that such differences are probably chance findings from uncorrected multiple comparisons, and notes that trail-making B and California verbal learning, which it says are often impaired, did not differ.

As described: with moderate use defined as fewer than 50 and heavy use as 50 or more lifetime occasions, the two subgroups did not generally differ and on some measures the moderate subgroup scored lower; only 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions, and the subgroups' lifetime use was not reported. The grooved pegboard did not differ with the dominant hand; with the non-dominant hand the whole ecstasy group was slower (P=0.02) and the heavier subgroup more so (P=0.003 against controls), which the study's authors judged probably chance.

As described by the commentary: of 15 neuropsychological tests, chosen because other studies had reported differences on them, only the Revised Strategy Applications Test clearly showed poorer performance, in the heavier-use subgroup but not the moderate one; the ecstasy group was selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, controls came from the same all-night-dance scene, and the analyses adjusted for demographic factors and childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

The commentary argues that poorer strategic self-regulation fits traits that precede drug use: lower serotonergic function has been linked to impulsivity, impulsivity to lower prefrontal activation, reward sensitivity and heavier substance use, and one prospective study found that decision-making performance in people who had not used ecstasy predicted later first use.

The review describes three studies of people with minimal other drug use: in a 2004 pilot study the lighter subgroup did not differ from controls while the heavier subgroup scored lower on Wisconsin card sorting, Stroop interference and a strategy test; in a Hong Kong study that excluded people with illicit polydrug histories, basic working memory was normal and verbal memory, non-verbal memory and complex attention were poorer; for the 2011 study the review says the whole group had few differences and attributes spatial span forwards and digit span backwards to the heavier subgroup, which the study's own tables do not show (see the card's reporting issues).
Before any ecstasy use, the 58 people who later started and the 60 who did not showed no differences on any of the 12 test scores (multivariate F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08).

tasks.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of the Sample and Substance Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Other substances: cannabis higher in the ecstasy group at baseline (48.8 vs 17.2 joints in the last year, p = .04) and at follow-up (53.6 vs 20.5, p < .001), cocaine higher at follow-up (1.4 vs 0.3 times, p = .006); smoking, alcohol, amphetamines and cocaine similar at baseline.
Overall test performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population.

tasks.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 732) and 6th paragraph (begins p. 733)
tasks.extracted: The authors list alternatives to an ecstasy effect: cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine use, sensation seeking (higher in people who started using ecstasy in the wider cohort), depression and expectancy from the information given at entry; and limitations: no indisputable evidence of causality, self-reported medical history, unmeasured lifestyle and settings, longer follow-up for controls (argued not to explain the result because retest effects shrink with time), uncontrolled tablet content and a well-educated, motivated sample.

As summarized: of 149 people almost naive to ecstasy at baseline, 23 who had used a mean of 13.5 tablets over the following year were compared with 43 people who used cannabis; most tasks did not differ, but figural visual recognition (immediate and delayed) was poorer (Wagner et al., 2013). Of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, 58 who then used an average of 3.2 tablets were compared with 60 who did not; there was no neurocognitive difference at baseline, and at follow-up the ecstasy group had poorer immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition (Schilt et al., 2007). The review gives the retest interval as 18-36 months, which is wrong by the editors' check against the primary paper (Schilt et al., 2007, PDF p. 731: mean 11.1 months in the ecstasy group and 19.1 months in the control group).

As summarized: 15 people tested a year apart, whose average lifetime use rose from 19 to 55 occasions, declined on Rivermead paragraph recall but not on two Wechsler subtests; at 2 years, the 8 who had stopped were unchanged or better (overall Rivermead memory score 19.9 to 22.9) and the 7 who continued were unchanged or worse (17.4 to 9.2). There was no retested comparison group, so practice effects cannot be separated from change.

As summarized from the same prospective programme: 188 people who had not used ecstasy were followed, and the 59 who had used it by the 17-month follow-up (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) were compared with 56 who had not; serotonin transporter binding did not differ, which the review attributes to the very low use, while measures of cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion differed (de Win et al., 2008).

tasks.extracted: Current vs abstinent (at least 6 months): no difference in overall learning and memory, g 0.03 (95% CI -0.35 to 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77%, unchanged when the poor-quality cohort was excluded; verbal and visual subtests also near zero (g -0.17 to 0.24, all intervals including zero).

tasks.extracted: Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall learning and memory g -1.37 (95% CI -2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; current vs MDMA-naive: g -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%.

tasks.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (last sentence)
tasks.extracted: Because of the small sample, the effect of longer durations of abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested.

Of the three learning-and-memory studies not pooled, two case-control studies found impairment despite 12 to 24 months of abstinence, while a small 2-year prospective study of poor quality found memory improved in people who stopped and worsened in people who continued (Zakzanis and Campbell, 2006).

tasks.locator: Results › Executive function, 1st paragraph (begins p. 279, continues p. 280)
tasks.extracted: Executive function (10 studies): the two prospective studies (poor quality) found neither improvement nor deterioration after 18 months of abstinence; seven case-control studies found no significant difference between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; four by the same author with the same abstinent participants showed a trend for abstinent groups to score between current-use groups and controls.

Quality: all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies rated poor, 5 fair; comparability of abstinent and control groups questioned in all studies and matching in all case-control studies; exposure assessed by self-report in 12 of 14.

tasks.locator: Results › Patterns of MDMA use and other drug use, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276, continues p. 279)
tasks.extracted: Polysubstance use: in all studies both MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too; two used alcohol- and tobacco-using controls, and only one (Taurah et al., 2014) a completely drug-naive comparison group.

tasks.locator: Results › Duration of abstinence (p. 279); Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins p. 281, continues p. 282)
tasks.extracted: Abstinence minima: 6 months in 8 studies, 12 months in 1, 18 months in 2, 24 months in 2, 48 months in 1; the study with the lowest exposure (mean 36 to 69 tablets) also had the longest abstinence, so dose and abstinence are confounded across studies; no dose-response analysis was done.

The authors state that their results do not definitively confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the conclusions rest on variable, low-quality findings, and that pre-existing traits may explain differences.

tasks.locator: §2.2 'Serotonergic neurotoxicity' in humans: neuroimaging findings, 2nd paragraph (proof lines 186-210)
tasks.extracted: As summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 people who did not use it; serotonin transporter binding lower in every cortical region (range -19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to years of use and maximum dose; recent use checked by hair analysis, with other drug use, sex, a gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored; the occipital lobe showed the largest mean reduction (46%) in a caudorostral gradient (Kish et al., 2010).

As summarized: a group who preferred MDMA showed lower serotonin transporter binding potential in the neocortex (-56%), pallidostriatum (-19%) and amygdala (-32%), with the extent correlated with lifetime MDMA exposure, while a group who preferred hallucinogens (mainly LSD) showed no change (Erritzoe et al., 2011); a post-mortem case of one person who had used ecstasy as well as cocaine and heroin had striatal serotonin 60% to 77% below normal with normal dopamine (Kish et al., 2000).

The review states that not every imaging study found reductions, that the variation has been attributed to lifetime dose, duration of abstinence, radioligand, brain region, sex, polydrug use and sample size, and that the early evidence was criticized in the mid-2000s over the specificity of the markers for serotonin and other methodological issues, before reviews concluded that lower serotonin transporter density was the most robust finding.

As summarized: in a prospective cohort, the 59 people who had used ecstasy by the 17-month follow-up (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) did not differ in serotonin transporter binding from 56 people who had not, which the review attributes to the very low lifetime dose; the study's authors concluded that they could not exclude that even low doses are neurotoxic, and reported differences in cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion.

tasks.locator: 8th paragraph (p. 1366 right column, continued on p. 1367)
tasks.extracted: As summarized by the letter: a review of the neuroimaging literature (the letter's reference 23) concluded that reduced serotonin transporter density was the most robust finding; a study of 49 people abstinent from ecstasy and 50 people who did not use it found binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and the hippocampus (-21%), associated with cumulative lifetime use and maximum use on one occasion, persisting after control for confounds including other drug use, and correlated with cognitive performance.

The author of a cross-sectional imaging study writes that MDMA has a well-established ability to cause serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates and that he is not aware of evidence that humans are less vulnerable, while accepting that traits such as impulsivity may predispose people to use MDMA; he gives no human measurement in support.

As summarized in the Discussion (studies not read): a meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies found lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, with a positive association with time abstinent that rested largely on one small study (Muller et al., 2019); one study of people abstinent 2.5 years found possible transporter recovery without recovery of verbal memory (Thomasius et al., 2006).

As the authors describe the 2002 study: published in Science in September 2002 by Ricaurte, McCann and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University, funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse; MDMA was given to 10 non-human primates to model human use; imaging was reported to show severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity, and the authors of the case study state that two of the animals died. The dopaminergic finding was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism.

As described: in September 2003, one year after publication, Science issued a retraction in which Ricaurte and colleagues wrote that they had discovered that methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been used to treat all but one study animal, because of a labelling error; the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies then asked the funding institute to investigate all work done by the group since the mislabelled supply had been received.

Of 50 newspapers, 26 (52%) published a report on the publication and 20 (40%) on the retraction; 6 (12%) covered the retraction without having covered the publication; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction. Circulation size was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84).

Mean word count 482 (SD 303; range 69 to 1260) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193; range 86 to 837) for retraction stories; in the 14 newspapers covering both events, 550 (SD 271) against 386 (SD 205). No test of these differences is reported.

All 20 retraction stories reported that the original findings had suggested that one night's MDMA use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism, and that a mix-up of study compounds had made the results erroneous. Fewer gave context: 14 (70%) mentioned long-standing controversy, 13 (65%) earlier criticism, 11 (55%) that animals died, 7 (35%) earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage, 7 (35%) allegations of political motives and 4 (20%) a quotation from a critic. No component differed significantly between the 14 newspapers covering both events and the 6 covering only the retraction (Fisher's exact test, p from 0.06 to 1.00).

tasks.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column); Response, 1st paragraph (middle column)
tasks.extracted: Three months before the retraction, critics argued that the high mortality among the primates showed the regimen was not a common recreational one and called the interspecies scaling into question; the study's authors replied that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies and that one of ten monkeys given the regimen had died of complications related to hyperthermia, from which they judged it premature to draw conclusions about mortality.

The authors note that the publication was accompanied by a university announcement and a press release from the publisher's association, that the retraction was issued late on a Friday afternoon, giving low-key coverage (quoting a journal editorial), and list as limitations that archives could not be searched for all of the 50 largest US newspapers, that the press release for the retraction could not be obtained, and that the placement of stories within newspapers was not analysed.

tasks.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column), middle of the paragraph
tasks.extracted: The critics state that studies finding normal dopamine, with reduced serotonin, in people who used MDMA heavily were not cited by the primate paper: two studies using in vivo imaging of the dopamine transporter and one post-mortem examination of one person; and that earlier studies by the same research group in people who used MDMA heavily did not find reduced dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid.

The study's authors reply that because the human studies cited did not take patterns of use into account, the groups were probably heterogeneous and dopamine markers, including the transporter, would not be expected to differ; and that cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity, so it would not be expected to be reduced even in a homogeneous group.

The authors state that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not materialized since the retraction, and that regulatory agencies have judged MDMA's potential therapeutic benefits to outweigh its risks in research settings; the only source given for these sentences is a 2014 commentary co-authored by one of them.

The dopaminergic finding in the 2002 primate study was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism after recreational use; the paper was retracted in September 2003 because, as its authors then reported, a labelling error meant that all but one animal had received methamphetamine rather than MDMA.

CSF HVA (a dopamine metabolite): 27.4 (21.3; range 8.1 to 117.9) in controls vs 19.4 (7.8) ng/ml; group F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01, group x gender F(1, 52) = 4.3, p = .04; lower only in MDMA women than control women (18.7 vs 34.8, control SD 29.9), not in men (22.1 vs 24.6). MHPG did not differ (8.5 vs 8.5).

The review states that serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is well established in laboratory animals, that imaging studies have found lower serotonin transporter binding in abstinent people who use ecstasy, that declarative memory, prospective memory and higher cognitive skills are often impaired, that the differences are often related to lifetime dose, with slight changes in light use and more pronounced problems in heavy use, and that abstinent people who use ecstasy can show deficits across a wide range of functions with a serotonergic component.

tasks.locator: §6.2 MDMA and serotonergic neurotoxicity: current explanatory model, 6th paragraph (proof lines 1522-1539)
tasks.extracted: The same review states that whether the problems endure over time cannot be answered on current evidence, that there are some indications that they endure but the empirical data are very limited, and that prospective studies combining neuroimaging with a comprehensive battery of functional measures are needed to address this question.

tasks.locator: §2.1 Serotonergic neurotoxicity in laboratory animals, 2nd paragraph (proof lines 141-158)
tasks.extracted: The review reports that the predominant hypothesis for the animal findings is loss of the end regions of long serotonin axons, that other interpretations including neuroadaptive change without terminal loss should be considered, and that the authors it cites called for a clearer definition of neurotoxicity while concluding that MDMA can be called neurotoxic in the sense of causing serotonergic dysfunction.

The letter concludes that the modest cognitive differences found in a study of people with minimal use of other drugs are congruent with current understanding of MDMA, that in the author's bio-energetic stress model MDMA is most damaging when taken intensively and cumulatively, and that the study confirms MDMA's potential for causing neurobiological damage even when taken carefully.

The commentary states that the evidence for functional signs of serotonergic neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy remains mixed, that transporter deficiencies in people who use ecstasy appear to recover with abstinence whereas they persist years after fenfluramine use, that the two possibilities cannot be disentangled in retrospective studies, and that within-person comparison before and after controlled exposure is the way to resolve it, the few such examples so far showing no resulting deficits.
tasks.quote: the chimera of MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in human ecstasy users may finally be put to rest

tasks.extracted: The author of a cross-sectional imaging study agrees with his critics on the need for well-controlled longitudinal studies to address the potential neurotoxic effects of recreational MDMA, and concludes that large, well-controlled prospective studies are needed to confirm or refute the findings of cross-sectional studies, while holding that well-designed cross-sectional studies remain informative.

The same author reports that his critics re-analysed his raw data by combining the MDMA group and the control group in one correlation and found no association between MDMA exposure and brain activation; he replies that people with little use tend to fall below the control mean and people with much use above it, so that including controls obscures the dose relationship. Neither analysis is given in numbers.

The authors state that debate continues about the safety of MDMA, including whether serotonergic damage associated with recreational use applies to pharmaceutical-grade MDMA and whether long-term neurocognitive deficits exist, citing among others the two 2011 commentaries and the reviews read in this batch.

Overall test performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population.

The authors state that their results do not definitively confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the conclusions rest on variable, low-quality findings, and that pre-existing traits may explain differences.

Only one included study was genuinely prospective (people tested before first ecstasy use); the others were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental, which makes it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences; the reviewers argue that prospective studies are slow and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical.
